Therefore, we proposed that ezetimibe, a lipid-lowering drug, and sericin, a natural silk protein with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, were evaluated for their potential to mitigate CdCl2-induced neurotoxicity in experimental rats. Seventy adult Wistar rats were allocated to receive control, CdCl2 (5 mg/kg), CdCl2 with ezetimibe (10 and 20 mg/kg), and sericin (200 and 400 mg/kg), or in combination for 28 days. Behavioral assessments, muscle coordination, and cognitive dysfunction were performed. Animals were sacrificed on day 29, and hippocampal tissue was used to perform oxidative stress markers, including malondialdehyde (MDA), nitrite, glutathione (GSH), estimation of acetylcholinesterase, and neurochemicals (serotonin, norepinephrine), neuroinflammatory markers, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1beta (IL-1β), nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), immunohistochemistry of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), mitochondrial complex-I activity, and protein expression of IGF-1R, GLP-1R, Nrf2, NF-κB, and HO-1. CdCl2 exposure resulted in motor and cognitive deficits, increased oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Ezetimibe and sericin, specifically the combination group, showed more pronounced effects; they improved motor behavior, maintained redox homeostasis, restored neurotransmitter levels, reduced neuroinflammation, and increased mitochondrial complex-I activity. Moreover, they restored the protein expression of IGF-1R, GLP-1R, Nrf2, NF-κB, and HO-1. The results demonstrate that ezetimibe and sericin, alone and in combination, can counteract Cd2+-induced neurotoxicity.

title: How Does Sleep Deprivation Rewrite the Cognitive Function in the Hippocampus?
abstract: In the modern society, sleep loss has become a global concern. Sleep deprivation (SD), a special type of complete acute or chronic sleep loss, swiftly erodes cognitive functions with observed structural and functional changes in the brain according to previous research. Hippocampus, especially its cornu ammonis 1 region presenting density in cognition-critical pyramidal neurons and complex inter-cellular crosstalk, is particularly vulnerable to sleep loss. SD disrupts hippocampal structure and function, leading to cognitive deficits. Mechanistically, by uncoupling energy-redox homeostasis, SD silences plasticity-promoting signals and neuron-glia interactions while amplifying neuroinflammation and metabolic deficits, thereby disrupting synaptic efficacy, network synchrony, waste removal procedure, and neurogenesis across the hippocampus and its related circuits. Although several pharmacological and non-pharmacological translational attempts have been announced, more efforts are in demand for advanced multi-modal models and cohorts integrating transcriptomics, connectomics, and real-time neuromodulation for elucidating the cascading mechanisms of SD-induced cognitive deficits in the hippocampus, as well as for interventions restoring sleep-dependent cognitive resilience and supporting precision psychiatry.

title: Hypoxia-powered MRI guides supramaximal biosurgical sampling of glioblastoma infiltration: the GLIOXY initiative.
abstract: To assess the feasibility of using hypoxia-powered magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to guide prospective sampling of high-response habitats beyond contrast enhancement in glioblastoma. Nine treatment-naive patients with histologically confirmed isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-wildtype glioblastoma underwent blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) MRI during a controlled transient hypoxic stimulus on the evening before surgery. Anatomical segmentation and voxel-wise temporal decomposition generated normalized hypoxia response maps. Otsu thresholding defined a high-response habitat outside contrast enhancement. Targets were confirmed with the surgeon according to anatomical accessibility and eloquence, transferred to neuronavigation, and sampled before major debulking. We divided the specimen for formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded neuropathology and frozen-tissue storage. Neuronavigation transfer succeeded in all nine cases. Eight targets were accessible and sampled. Seven sampled targets contained tumor. One yielded reactive cortex and white matter without definite tumor. No target-sampling complications were observed among the eight sampled procedures. Hypoxia-powered MRI could be integrated into prospective neuronavigation-guided sampling beyond contrast enhancement. Tumor was identified in seven of eight sampled targets. By translating a tracer-free physiological response map into coordinate-matched tissue, the GLIOXY workflow enables prospective, targeted tissue sampling of non-enhancing glioblastoma regions.

title: Dealing with the self in empirical cognitive science: a case study of four conceptual approaches.
abstract: Cognitive science has a persistent interest in understanding the self, yet researchers often use the term in different ways and for different explanatory purposes. Drawing on conceptual analyses conducted within the German Research Foundation (DFG) Priority Program The Active Self, this article presents a case study of how concepts of the self are operationalized in interdisciplinary empirical research. Project members were invited to describe the concepts of self guiding their research, and these descriptions were synthesized into a set of recurring conceptual categories. This analysis identified four recurring uses of the concept of self: as a naïve theory, as a placeholder for agent-related implicit knowledge, as phenomenal experience, and as a carrier of psychological function. We argue that these uses should not be understood as competing empirical theories of the same entity. Rather, they differ in the explanatory role assigned to the self, namely as explanandum, explanans, operational placeholder, or phenomenological target. Analysis of these roles reveals conceptual tensions that arise when they are conflated, including reification, category mistakes, and pseudo-mechanistic explanation. We suggest that greater clarity regarding the explanatory function of self concepts can facilitate interdisciplinary communication and theoretical integration. More generally, this case study illustrates how conceptual heterogeneity within collaborative research programs can impede integration when underlying assumptions remain implicit.

title: Cladribine in data-driven secondary progressive multiple sclerosis: an Italian registry analysis.
Neural correlates underlying motor sequence task performance: handedness and sequence complexity.
abstract: We aimed to determine the neural correlates of motor sequence performance in healthy young adults, with respect to handedness and sequence complexity. Strongly left-handed (LH, n = 15, 24.9y) and right-handed (RH, n = 15, 26.4y) participants performed finger key presses on a numeric keypad at four levels of sequence complexity with each hand in a randomized order. Both LH and RH performed the motor sequence task with faster reaction and motor execution times when using their right hand, irrespective of sequence complexity. Increasing motor-sequence complexity reduced frontal and parietal EEG power in both LH and RH, particularly at the highest complexity level, while RH also showed increased occipital delta activity when using the non-dominant hand, indicating that both sequence complexity and handedness modulate cortical activity during motor sequence performance. In addition, connectivity analysis showed significant hemispheric differences in brain network organization across frequency bands, with mainly greater left-hemisphere frontal and occipital connectivity but stronger right-hemisphere parietal connectivity. Sequence complexity primarily influenced functional connectivity (wPLI) rather than network topology. Notably, connectivity measures and selected MST-derived graph-theoretical metrics were linked to motor performance. Our findings suggest that motor-sequence performance is faster with the right hand, regardless of handedness and sequence complexity, which relies on a consistently organized hemispheric network, while increasing task complexity is managed primarily through frequency-specific changes in functional connectivity rather than large-scale reorganization of network structure.

title: Self-harm rates amongst individuals from ethnic minority backgrounds: A global systematic review.
abstract: The evidence on ethnic variation in self-harm risk is growing. This systematic review is the first to synthesise the global epidemiological evidence on absolute and relative rates of self-harm in individuals from ethnic minority backgrounds (including migrant and Indigenous populations). We identified empirical evidence through database searches (Medline, Embase, and PsycINFO published between 01/01/2000-19/12/2023). Studies were included if they reported absolute and/or relative rates of non-fatal self-harm in general population samples from ethnic minority groups. Lifetime self-harm was excluded. Due to limitations in the available data by country, we present a narrative synthesis and forest plots of the rates only. Synthesis was further stratified by sex, migration status, and self-harm method (where possible). Quality assessment was conducted using modified Newcastle Ottawa Scales. CRD42021248646. We included 36 studies from 14 countries. Seven (19%) were of reasonable quality. Most were conducted in North America (15/36; 42%) and/or in high-income countries (33/36; 92%). Self-harm risk was elevated amongst certain Indigenous and migrant groups, though there was not always statistical evidence of elevated rates compared to the majority population. High heterogeneity was present. The available evidence was of low quality and heterogeneous, indicating a need for improved reporting of self-harm by ethnicity and nuanced understanding of intersecting factors such as place of birth and migratory status. Appropriate surveillance, particularly in South America and Africa, is required to better understand international variations in self-harm prevalence for ethnic minority groups and inform population health suicide prevention.

title: Discontinuation and optimization of device-aided therapies in Parkinson's disease: a prospective comparative real-world study.
abstract: Comparative real-world evidence on device-aided therapy (DAT) persistence in Parkinson's disease (PD) is limited. We assessed discontinuation, reasons, optimization time, and associated factors. We analyzed the prospective multicenter DATs-PD GETM Spanish Registry (January 2024-May 2026), including deep brain stimulation (DBS), continuous subcutaneous apomorphine infusion (CSAI), foslevodopa/foscarbidopa (fLD/fCD), levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG), and levodopa-entacapone-carbidopa intestinal gel (LECIG). Persistence and associated factors were examined using Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression analyses. Among 565 patients receiving 591 DATs, 170 (28.8%) treatments were discontinued: DBS 4.1% (4/97), CSAI 34.1% (45/132), fLD/fCD 34.7% (101/291), LCIG 28.6% (4/14), and LECIG 28.1% (16/57). Among infusion therapies, discontinuation was 33.6%, without significant differences in rates (p = 0.774) or Kaplan-Meier persistence (p = 0.701). Main reasons were adverse events (38.2%) and patient decision (25.3%). Mean optimization time was 61.6 ± 97.2 days (LECIG 19.6 ± 33.1; DBS 115.2 ± 118.3). Discontinuation was associated with institutional caregiving (HR 5.162, 95% CI 1.441-18.490), higher ON-state Hoehn and Yahr stage (HR 1.814, 95% CI 1.110-2.964), and longer daily OFF time (HR 1.093, 95% CI 1.002-1.193). Approximately one-third of infusion DATs were discontinued, with no significant persistence differences. Disease severity, OFF time, and caregiving environment were associated with discontinuation. Observational differences in selection and exposure preclude direct comparative-effectiveness conclusions.

title: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use in third trimester of pregnancy and birth outcomes after vaginal birth - a Swedish retrospective register study 2005-2015.
journal: Journal of psychosomatic obstetrics and gynaecology
abstract: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are prescribed for depression during pregnancy, yet the impact on maternal and neonatal outcomes remains insufficiently studied. The study aimed to describe the prevalence of prescribed SSRIs to pregnant women and its association with birth outcomes after a vaginal birth. A registry study included 405,936 term vaginal births in Sweden. SSRI prescriptions were identified. Crude and adjusted odds ratios with 99% confidence intervals were calculated, with statistical significance set at p 1000 mL. postpartum. Women prescribed SSRIs were more likely to give birth at 37-38 weeks' gestation and have neonates with head circumference < 35 cm and with Apgar score < 7 at 5 min. SSRI prescriptions increased significantly between 2005 and 2015 and were associated with higher risks of adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. Until more conclusive evidence is availble midwives and obstetricians should remain vigilant when supporting pregnant women with depression or anxiety, considering the potential risks of pharmacological treatment alongside non-pharmacological management of maternal mental health conditions.

title: The Art and Science of Neuroplastic and Reconstructive Surgery.
abstract: Neuroplastic and reconstructive surgery has emerged as a distinct discipline at the intersection of neurosurgery and plastic surgery, addressing the anatomic, functional, and psychosocial consequences of central and peripheral nervous system pathology in adult patients. This educational supplement presents a comprehensive overview of the field, spanning its history and founding principles, a novel anatomically based surgical complexity classification, multidisciplinary preoperative planning, radiation-induced scalp injury and the RadioScalp staging system, the reconstructive hierarchy for scalp defects, oncoplastic neurosurgery, neurotechnology-integrated cranial implants, prevention and salvage of neurosurgical complications, and the psychological and quality-of-life dimensions of cranial reconstruction. Contributions from leading surgeons across neurosurgery, plastic surgery, and craniofacial surgery illustrate how coordinated, multidisciplinary care improves complication rates, functional outcomes, and patient dignity. Together, these chapters establish a clinical and educational foundation for neuroplastic and reconstructive surgery as a maturing surgical subspecialty.

title: Developmental elimination of electrical synapses by UNC-51/UNC-76-mediated vesicular transport.
abstract: Neural circuit maturation requires precise elimination of transient synaptic connections, but how electrical synapses are eliminated remains unknown. Using Caenorhabditis elegans PLM mechanosensory neurons, we found that gap junctions form transiently during early development and are subsequently eliminated as the circuit matures. These transient electrical synapses drive high-frequency calcium oscillations; optogenetic ablation of early gap junctions abolishes calcium dynamics and disrupts chemical synapse formation, while restoring calcium activity independently of gap junction coupling substantially rescues this defect, directly linking electrical synapse-driven calcium dynamics to chemical synapse formation. Through forward genetic screening, we identified the conserved kinase UNC-51/ULK as essential for elimination. UNC-51 phosphorylates the kinesin adaptor UNC-76/FEZ to promote RAB-10-dependent net retrograde removal of innexins, progressively depleting innexin proteins from the synaptic site. Disrupting this pathway prevents elimination, causing persistent electrical synapses and neuronal hyperactivity. These findings establish a conserved framework for developmental elimination of functionally essential transient electrical connectivity.

title: Adolescent headache in a changing world: Diverging trends, shared challenges.
journal: Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore

title: Lecanemab in Singapore: Appropriate use recommendations for early Alzheimer's disease.
journal: Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore
abstract: Lecanemab, a monoclonal antibody targeting β-amyloid oligomers, protofibrils, and insoluble fibrils, has been approved for Alzheimer's disease (AD) treatment in Singapore, based on the phase 3 Clarity AD study. In this paper, the Singapore-adapted Appropriate Use Recommendations (AURs) serve to assist Singapore physicians in identifying patients who will likely benefit from treatment while ensuring effective monitoring. The AURs are based on the Singaporeapproved prescribing information combined with lecanemab phase 2 and 3 clinical trials and real-world data up to April 2026. The decision to initiate lecanemab should be based on careful evaluation of individuals, including Singapore-validated cognitive status tests to identify mild cognitive impairment (MCI) due to AD and mild AD dementia. Other important evaluations include baseline brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), assessment of the apolipoprotein E ε4 (APOEε4) genotype, and amyloid pathology confirmation. Guidance on identifying patients at increased risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) during treatment and other patient profiles warranting additional caution is provided. Recommendations for monitoring patients, managing infusion-related reactions, and identifying lecanemab discontinuation scenarios are included. Lecanemab should only be prescribed for patients with MCI due to AD or mild AD dementia following careful clinical evaluation confirming AD pathology, with caution exercised in patients at increased ARIA risk (e.g. APOEε4 gene carriers). During treatment, patients should receive regular monitoring for ARIA symptoms including follow-up MRI scans. Future directions include the development of a Singapore-specific registry to monitor patients and gather long-term data to support a consensus-driven framework to inform and optimise the use of lecanemab in Singapore.

title: Constructing events across perception, action, and thought.
abstract: The brain organizes continuous experience into events that structure episodic memory and guide behavior. Traditional accounts have primarily focused on sensory discontinuities and prediction errors that trigger updates of event models. Here, we broaden this view to consider event boundaries arising during goal-directed behavior, spontaneous thought, and memory recall, including transitions generated in the absence of corresponding changes in sensory input. We propose that prediction error and uncertainty provide complementary signals for event model updating: prediction errors signal a violation of current expectations, whereas uncertainty may promote updating when upcoming states become difficult to predict. We further suggest that the hippocampus may serve as a candidate hub linking boundary-related representational changes across perception, action, and thought. Together, this framework offers an integrative account of how the brain detects and generates event structure in continuous experience to support memory and behavior.

title: Weight Loss, FVC Decline, and Composite Physiologic Index as Complementary Prognostic Indicators in Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis over the Disease Course: Time-Updated and Landmark Analysis.
abstract: To evaluate the independent and combined prognostic impact of weight loss, disease severity, and forced vital capacity (FVC) decline in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) using time-updated and landmark analyses. We retrospectively analysed 2697 visits from 667 patients with IPF followed at a single tertiary centre. Annualised changes in body weight and FVC were calculated at each visit. Time updated flexible parametric survival models were used to assess associations with transplant-free survival, adjusting for disease severity (Composite Physiologic Index, CPI) and clinical covariates. Landmark analyses at 1-4 years and joint longitudinal survival models were also performed. In time-updated analyses, higher CPI (HR (95% CI): 2.75 (2.28-3.33)) per 10-point increase, ≥5% annual weight loss (HR: 1.85 (1.31-2.52)), and ≥10 percentage point annual decline in FVC% predicted (HR: 2.26 (1.66-3.10)) were independently associated with transplant-free survival. Patients meeting both thresholds for weight loss and FVC decline had a markedly increased risk (HR: 4.11 (2.65-6.40)), with no evidence of interaction. These findings were consistent across landmark analyses. Joint modelling confirmed their independent effect and showed that threshold-based changes were more strongly associated with transplant-free survival than continuous longitudinal trajectories. Reverse-time analysis suggested that the decline in both weight and FVC accelerates in the last months before death or transplant. Weight loss and FVC decline provide independent and additive prognostic information in IPF, with comparable effect sizes and consistency of the effect over time. Routine weight monitoring may improve risk stratification and help identify patients at high risk of adverse outcomes.

title: Consumer neuroscience: the emerging science of everyday choices.
abstract: Consumer neuroscience is a developing field at the intersection of neuroscience, psychology, economics, and marketing that seeks to uncover the neural and physiological mechanisms underlying consumer behavior. Building on early psychophysiological studies, the field has expanded substantially since the mid-2000s through an increasing range of methods and models. We highlight that its strength lies in spanning multiple levels of analysis to address marketing-relevant questions. We highlight four major trends driving the field: improving behavioral prediction, synthesizing evidence through multidataset analyses, developing formal models linking neural processes to consumer decision-making, and integrating brain and body measures. Together, these advances position consumer neuroscience as an integrative science with implications for marketing, policy, and consumer welfare.

title: Sociodemographic and clinical factors associated with comorbid dementia in late-life difficult-to-treat depression: A cross-sectional study using electronic health records.
abstract: Late-life difficult-to-treat depression (LL-DTD) is associated with dementia, but the factors associated with comorbid dementia in this population remain unknown. We aimed to identify sociodemographic and clinical factors associated with comorbid dementia in LL-DTD. Cross-sectional study using electronic mental health records from a south London mental healthcare provider. Patients aged ≥ 60 years with a first recorded depressive episode between 2008 and 2023, meeting criteria for LL-DTD (n = 3886). LL-DTD was defined as ≥ 2 antidepressants prescribed or a natural language processing algorithm indicating treatment resistance. Dementia was ascertained using ICD-10 codes. Sociodemographic characteristics, depressive symptoms, and physical health conditions were ascertained from the electronic health record. Multivariable logistic regression was used. A sensitivity analysis restricted dementia to diagnoses recorded more than three months after the index episode. Of 3886 patients with LL-DTD, 890 (22.9%) had dementia. Older age, female sex, and Black and Asian ethnicity were associated with higher odds of dementia (aOR 1.07, 1.24, 1.83 and 1.73, respectively). Somatic multimorbidity, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular conditions were also associated with higher odds. Anxiety (aOR 1.66) and cognitive problems (aOR 3.98) showed positive associations, while severe or psychotic depression and several ICD-10/11 depressive symptoms showed negative associations. When restricted to dementia recorded after the index episode, the association with cognitive problems halved (aOR 1.93) and those with apathy and ADL problems were lost. In our analysis, somatic multimorbidity, cardiovascular conditions and anxiety were associated with comorbid dementia in LL-DTD, supporting comprehensive physical and neuropsychiatric assessment.

title: Thalamic stereoEEG in epilepsy: from cortical dogma to network-based hypotheses.
The balance N1 attenuates but persists during self-initiated and repeated perturbations, even without active balance control.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Standing balance requires rapid responses to postural disturbances, and the balance N1 has been proposed to reflect cortical involvement in corrective motor output. Our recent work shows, however, that the N1 persists even when active balance control is removed and corrective muscle activity is largely absent, suggesting it reflects sensory rather than motor processing. Because the N1 is also modulated by contextual factors such as postural threat, stability, and perturbation predictability, it may reflect uncertainty associated with perturbation-evoked sensory signals. We tested this in 11 participants (3 males and 8 females) using toes-up perturbations across three manipulations expected to alter sensorimotor uncertainty: perturbation timing through 15 unexpected perturbations before and after a block of self-initiated trials; repeated exposure through 60 self-initiated trials; and body-motion variability by comparing active balance with passive support and by imposing prerecorded whole-body motion during 60 additional self-initiated trials with passive support. Self-initiation reduced N1 amplitude by 21.3 ± 13.9% relative to unexpected perturbations, and this attenuation was equivalent across active and passive conditions. Habituation through repeated self-initiated perturbations produced a further 24.0 ± 17.7% decline, again independent of active balance. When perturbations were subsequently delivered unexpectedly, N1 amplitudes increased, confirming that attenuation was specific to the self-initiated context. Finally, imposing prerecorded whole-body motion during passive support did not change perturbation-evoked N1 amplitude, suggesting that body-motion variability does not drive the cortical response when active balance control is absent. These results indicate that the balance N1 is shaped by predictability and repetition, consistent with prediction error or surprise-based accounts of cortical responses to balance perturbations.Significance statement The balance N1, a cortical response to postural disturbances, has long been thought to reflect corrective motor output. We recently showed it instead reflects sensory processing, as it persists even without active balance control. Here we test whether this processing scales with uncertainty associated with perturbation-evoked sensory signals by manipulating perturbation timing through self-initiation, habituation through repeated exposure, and variability of ongoing whole-body motion. Self-initiation and repetition both attenuated N1, regardless of whether participants actively balanced or were passively supported. However, increasing whole-body motion variability did not modify the response, indicating that not all sources of uncertainty modulate the N1. These findings recast the balance N1 as tracking the sensory predictability of the perturbation, not balance-correcting motor output.

title: A spectral partial information decomposition framework for quantifying information about cognitive variables in oscillatory brain networks.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Neural oscillations are thought to play a central role in encoding and transmitting cognitive information across large-scale brain networks, yet the relative contributions of phase synchrony and amplitude co-modulations to distributed coding remain unclear. A key obstacle is the absence of tools that can simultaneously quantify task-relevant information in the frequency domain and disentangle its phase and amplitude co-modulation components across pairwise and higher order interactions. Here, we introduce a spectral partial information decomposition framework (NeOPID) for quantifying information about cognitive variables in amplitude co-modulation and phase contributions, and to quantify redundant and synergistic information in brain relations, from pairwise to higher-order interactions. We validated the approach on Kuramoto and Stuart- Landau oscillator networks, including a whole-brain model constrained by macaque anatomical connectivity. NeOPID accurately recovers ground-truth encoding schemes and reveals that phase relations and amplitude co-modulations act as complementary coding channels with both redundant and synergistic components. NeOPID further extends this decomposition to higher-order functional interactions enabling the characterization of how cognitive information is collectively distributed across multiple oscillatory edges via redundant and synergistic encoding. To illustrate biological applicability, we applied NeOPID to local field potentials (LFPs) recorded from the macaque fronto-parietal network during a working memory task. In this dataset, NeOPID identified beta-band amplitude co-modulations as the primary carrier of stimulus information, and revealed that higher-order phase interactions exhibit both redundant and synergistic structure during the memory delay. These results establish NeOPID as a principled tool for dissecting the informational architecture about cognitive processes of oscillatory brain networks.Significance Statement Understanding how the brain coordinates large-scale communication to support cognition remains a fundamental challenge in neuroscience. Characterizing the distinct roles of phase synchrony and amplitude co-modulation has been hindered by a lack of computational approaches capable of separating these components across pairwise and higher-order interactions. Here, we introduce NeOPID (neural spectral Partial Information Decomposition), a framework designed to isolate phase and amplitude co-modulation contributions and quantify redundant and synergistic information contained in pair-wise and higher order functional interactions. NeOPID was validated on simulated oscillator models and on macaque local field potentials (LFPs) during a working memory task. Overall, the results establish NeOPID as a principled tool for dissecting the informational architecture underlying cognitive processes in oscillatory brain networks.

title: Gaze reinstatement during working memory for natural scenes.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: The information we hold in mind with working memory (WM) may propagate beyond the cortex and out to the peripheral motor system. For instance, directionally biased hand and eye movements can express simple visuo-spatial features during WM maintenance. If such sensorimotor inflections are a form of WM representation, they may also express more detailed and task-adaptive information about WM content. Here, we ask whether gaze patterns carry item-specific detail about complex stimuli held in mind, and whether gaze during WM maintenance adapts to upcoming behavioral demands. To do this, we tracked male and female human eye movements during WM for naturalistic images, and we manipulated which image properties were most task-relevant (visual or semantic). In two experiments, we found that the eyes moved in item-specific spatiotemporal sequences during WM maintenance. Delay period gaze patterns retraced the scanpaths from stimulus encoding, echoing the 'gaze reinstatement' that has been observed during long-term memory retrieval. Therefore, gaze patterns during WM may reinstate visual encoding processes for maintenance. We also used time-resolved representational similarity analyses, guided by convolutional neural network modeling, to test the specificity of WM gaze patterns across a trial. We found that gaze representations were more distinct when the task prioritized visual detail, and they also ramped up in anticipation of the WM probe. Therefore, oculomotor WM signals are malleable to when and how the content will be used. WM may recruit the most primary structures in sensorimotor processing, where eye movements reflect flexible and future-oriented WM content information.Significance Statement The eyes are an outwardly accessible extension of the brain. They filter sensory input and enact motor output, but may also offer a rich window into underlying cognition. For instance, pupil dilation can reflect changing cognitive load, and biased eye movements can reflect basic spatial information about content held in mind with working memory (WM). WM is a critical neuro-cognitive function, but its physiological bases remain under debate. Here, we show that during WM the eyes can move in intricate patterns that read out the complex, real-world stimuli held in mind. This work shows how cognitive states influence oculomotor functions, and also advances theories of WM maintenance to include the most basic structures in sensorimotor processing.

title: Cell-type- and subregion-specific basolateral amygdala inputs to ventral CA1-subiculum.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: The hippocampus is essential for learning and memory and interacts extensively with cortical and subcortical regions. Although the heterogeneity of intrinsic connectivity of hippocampal neurons is well established, the diversity of its extrahippocampal connectivity remains less understood. Such differential connectivity may contribute to functional diversity of hippocampal neurons in specific positions. Ventral CA1 (vCA1) and ventral subiculum (vSub) form strong reciprocal connections with the basolateral amygdala (BLA), a region critical for emotional and social regulation. Consequently, BLA-vCA1-vSub circuits have been implicated in anxiety-related and social behaviors. However, the functional connectivity from BLA to vCA1-vSub at the cellular and circuit levels is underexplored. To address this, we combined viral tracing with Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2)-assisted slice electrophysiology to examine BLA projections to vCA1-vSub in mice of either sex. We found that BLA inputs are not uniformly distributed along the transverse axis in vCA1-vSub. Instead, BLA selectively excites pyramidal neurons in distal vCA1-vSub while largely avoiding proximal vCA1 near CA2. BLA terminals strongly excited parvalbumin-expressing interneurons but only weakly recruited a small subset of somatostatin-expressing interneurons, generating robust disynaptic inhibitory synaptic currents in pyramidal neurons. Additionally, the same distal pyramidal neurons that receive BLA excitation also project back to the BLA. These findings reveal that BLA establishes cell-type- and subregion-specific excitatory connections within vCA1-vSub, highlighting a circuit architecture that may underlie functional heterogeneity in ventral hippocampal processing.Significance statement The hippocampus interacts extensively with cortical and subcortical regions, yet how long-range extrahippocampal inputs are organized across hippocampal subregions remains poorly understood. We examined projections from the basolateral amygdala (BLA) to the ventral hippocampus and found that BLA inputs selectively excite pyramidal neurons in distal ventral CA1 and ventral subiculum while largely avoiding proximal ventral CA1. BLA projections preferentially excite parvalbumin-expressing interneurons, provide disynaptic inhibition onto pyramidal neurons, and are reciprocally connected with the same pyramidal neurons in ventral CA1 and subiculum they excite. These findings reveal a highly selective connectivity pattern of amygdala-hippocampal circuits, providing a circuit framework for understanding how emotional information is routed through distinct ventral hippocampal pathways.

title: AgRP neurons as an integrative node linking the somatotropic and reproductive axes.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Growth hormone (GH) signaling contributes to pubertal development and reproductive function, yet the hypothalamic circuits mediating these effects remain incompletely understood. Kisspeptin and agouti-related protein (AgRP) neurons are key integrators of metabolic and reproductive cues and exhibit GH-responsive signaling pathways. We therefore investigated their contributions to the reproductive consequences of altered somatotropic signaling. Using genetic mouse models of chronic GH excess or deficiency, we examined the impact of altered GH signaling on pubertal maturation, fertility, and hypothalamic neuroendocrine function. Pubertal onset was unaffected in female mice, whereas males with either GH excess or GH deficiency exhibited delayed puberty. In contrast, GH hypersecretion selectively disrupted estrous cyclicity and impaired fertility in females. Female reproductive dysfunction occurred despite preserved kisspeptin signaling, as evidenced by the preservation of intrinsic electrophysiological properties of kisspeptin neurons and unaltered hypothalamic Kiss1 mRNA expression. Chronic GH excess increased hypothalamic Agrp mRNA expression and reduced Pomc and Tac2 mRNA expression compared to control mice; these transcriptional changes were prevented by AgRP-specific GH receptor (GHR) deletion, which also improved ovarian function. Notably, selective deletion of the GHR in AgRP cells markedly improved fertility in GH-hypersecreting females. Together, these findings identify AgRP neurons as a critical hypothalamic target through which chronic GH excess impairs female reproductive function. Our results further demonstrate that GH-induced infertility occurs independently of canonical kisspeptin-GnRH dysfunction, revealing a sexually dimorphic mechanism linking somatotropic signaling to reproductive competence.Significance Statement Reproductive dysfunction is a common consequence of chronic alterations in growth hormone (GH) secretion, but the underlying neural mechanisms remain poorly defined. We show that chronic GH excess induces a sexually dimorphic reproductive phenotype characterized by profound impairment of female fertility despite largely preserved kisspeptin neuronal function. In contrast, GH excess altered hypothalamic AgRP-associated pathways, and the selective deletion of GH receptors in AgRP neurons significantly improved fertility in GH-hypersecreting females. These findings identify AgRP neurons as key mediators of GH-induced reproductive dysfunction and reveal a previously unrecognized sexually dimorphic neuroendocrine mechanism linking somatotropic signaling, metabolic circuits, and female fertility.

title: Learning rapidly reshapes brain microstructure: evidence from dense temporal sampling of diffusion MRI.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Learning is associated with rapid microstructural changes in the human brain, yet the precise temporal dynamics of these changes remain unclear. Using dense temporal sampling of diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI) combined with task-based fMRI, we assessed microstructural changes throughout a declarative learning paradigm and subsequent rest. Seventy-four participants (36 females) learned image-location associations across four encoding-retrieval repetitions while undergoing interleaved functional and DW-MRI acquisitions. A matched control group (N=37, 21 females) underwent a similar imaging protocol without learning. Dense sampling of DW-MRI acquisitions (2146 images across 22 time points in 127 min) revealed that learning-induced mean diffusivity (MD) decreases emerged shortly after learning onset and continued to develop during post-learning rest. The most robust change was localized to the left middle occipital/temporal gyrus, a region also showing functional activation during encoding and retrieval. Linear mixed-effects modeling further confirmed a significant group-by-time interaction, with MD reductions in the left middle occipital/temporal gyrus emerging as early as ≈7 min after learning onset, becoming robust by ≈35-40 min, and persisting throughout the extended post-learning period, while controls showed no changes. Our findings demonstrate that learning-related microstructural plasticity unfolds continuously from encoding to offline consolidation, with learning-induced structural changes emerging in functionally engaged regions. Dense temporal sampling of DW-MRI offers a powerful approach to bridge functional activation and structural remodeling, providing evidence of when and where experience-dependent plasticity occurs during memory formation.Significance Statement How quickly does the brain's structure change when we learn? Using dense temporal sampling of diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI; 2146 images) across more than 2 hours, we show that microstructural plasticity arises rapidly during learning and continues to develop during post-learning rest. These learning-induced changes are spatially precise and overlap with task-related functional activity. By capturing the entire progression of microstructural plasticity across the learning process, rather than just before and after a learning paradigm, our study provides insights into when and where learning-induced plasticity occurs, demonstrating that memory formation involves rapid, ongoing microstructural changes in functionally engaged regions.

title: Venous Outflow Imaging in Acute Ischemic Stroke: An ASFNR State of Practice.
abstract: Venous outflow (VO) imaging describes the egress limb of the cerebral collateral circulation and has been associated with outcome in acute ischemic stroke; its added value beyond arterial collaterals and perfusion measures remains uncertain. More than a dozen VO measures have been proposed on CT and MR techniques used in acute stroke, spanning three physical signals: venous opacification, venous transit and venous oxygenation. They differ in what they measure, in evidence maturity and in readiness for reporting. A writing group reviewed the peer-reviewed studies of cerebral venous drainage measures in acute ischemic stroke. The scope is CT and MRI obtained during routine acute stroke evaluation, excluding measures that require catheter angiography or ultrasound. We describe each measure's acquisition, definition, evidence and technical limitations, and propose a reporting framework based on these features. VO markers are descriptive prognostic measures, not treatment-selection criteria. The cortical vein opacification score (COVES) has the most mature CTA evidence and may be considered when venous timing is adequate, though meta-analyses support an association rather than a threshold; comprehensive venous outflow (CVO) adds the internal cerebral vein. Prolonged venous transit (PVT) adds a temporal dimension read from perfusion, but remains investigational, as do the composite arterial-venous scores, quantitative venous timing and oxygen extraction fraction mapping. Susceptibility signs index deoxygenation and venous blood volume, not drainage. Reporting should name the technique and describe opacification, transit or oxygenation findings in their own terms. The evidence base is predominantly anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion imaged before thrombectomy.

title: Cognitive function and return to work: protocol for a longitudinal study investigating cognitive endurance in patients with stress-related disorders in primary health care in Sweden.
Effects of opioid-free and opioid-sparing anesthesia on postoperative delirium: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a common neurocognitive condition linked with increased morbidity, long-term cognitive decline, and death. Perioperative opioid exposure may contribute to delirium through sedation, neuroinflammation, and neurotransmitter dysregulation. Opioid-free anesthesia and opioid-sparing anesthesia using agents such as ketamine, esketamine, and dexmedetomidine have emerged as a potential strategy to reduce POD. This meta-analysis evaluated the effects of opioid-free and opioid-sparing anesthetic regimens on POD in adult surgical patients. Embase, PubMed, and Web of Science were searched from inception to April 2026. Randomized controlled trials comparing ketamine-, esketamine-, or dexmedetomidine-based opioid-free and opioid-sparing strategies with placebo, conventional opioid-based anesthesia, or standard care were included. The primary outcome was POD. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using a random-effects model. Forty-one randomized controlled trials involving 7852 patients were analyzed. POD occurred in 488 of 4013 patients receiving opioid-free/opioid-sparing interventions and 633 of 3839 controls. Overall, these strategies significantly reduced the risk of delirium (RR = 0.641, 95% CI: 0.525-0.784; I2 = 52.2%). Subgroup analyses showed reductions with esketamine (RR = 0.745, 95% CI: 0.526-1.053) and dexmedetomidine (RR = 0.612, 95% CI: 0.471-0.796), while ketamine demonstrated a nonsignificant trend toward benefit (RR = 0.598, 95% CI: 0.251-1.423). No significant publication bias was detected. Opioid-free and opioid-sparing anesthetic strategies reduce POD in adult surgical patients, with dexmedetomidine and esketamine showing the most consistent benefits. These findings support multimodal opioid-sparing anesthesia for perioperative neurocognitive protection.

title: High-Throughput Plasma Proteomic Profiling Identifies Novel Biomarker Candidates in Parkinson's Disease with Cognitive Decline.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disease diagnosed based on its cardinal motor features. Many PD patients experience non-motor symptoms, including cognitive decline, which can be particularly debilitating. Fluid biomarkers in PD are lacking, but modern proteomic techniques have allowed for high-throughput studies which have generated promising results. Mass spectrometry provides an unbiased approach to biomarker discovery, and the plasma proteome reflects ongoing disease processes throughout the body, including the central nervous system. Plasma samples from 198 individuals (130 PD and 68 controls) from the Swedish Biopark cohort were TMT-tagged, pre-fractionated, and analysed using untargeted mass spectrometry. Robust peptides from candidate biomarkers were technically verified using parallel reaction monitoring (PRM). The analyses focused on PD diagnosis and cognitive decline. Results were compared with plasma Neurofilament light chain levels analysed on the SIMOA platform. Several promising candidate biomarkers were discovered for PD diagnosis, cognitive decline, and motor impairment in the discovery phase. Peptides from six of the 12 proteins quantified with PRM correlated with quantifications from the discovery phase. Following PRM verification, it was found that peptides from C9 and APOC3 had altered levels in PD compared with controls. Additionally, SAA1 was found to be associated with both cognitive and motor impairment. Neurofilament light chain levels were elevated in PD with cognitive impairment but showed a weaker correlation with cognitive function than SAA1. In conclusion, untargeted mass spectrometry is a viable method for generating novel candidate biomarkers in PD plasma, several of which were technically verified with PRM including SAA1, C9, and APOC3.

title: Reply to Comment on "Exposure to low-dose ionizing radiation and dementia mortality in Canadian nuclear power plant workers".
Enriched environment protects from high-fat diet-induced obesity but not from insulin resistance, glucose intolerance, and metabolic deterioration in the brain.
abstract: We investigated how an active lifestyle can compensate for poor nutrition. Male mice were either housed in an enriched environment (EE) or under control conditions and received either a high-fat diet (HFD) or a normal chow diet. EE markedly attenuated HFD-induced weight gain and prevented gain of fat mass. However, mice on HFD developed glucose intolerance and insulin resistance regardless of housing conditions. Already one day after onset of the intervention, EE and HFD modulated glucose uptake in feeding-related brain regions. Chronic HFD evoked a considerable reduction of brain glucose metabolism and induced meta-inflammation in the brain, which both were ameliorated by the EE. Following EE withdrawal, HFD-fed mice exhibited rapid weight gain and an elevated ratio of energy intake to expenditure. HFD was associated with increased DeltaFosB expression in the nucleus accumbens and dorsal striatum, brain regions related to reward-driven control of feeding. Our data show that an active lifestyle can only partially compensate for HFD-induced deficits in brain metabolism and inflammation and causes possible detrimental effects to the energy balance after cessation of the activity/exercise paradigm.

title: Prenatal cocaine exposure alters synaptic plasticity of hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons in postnatal rats.
abstract: Prenatal cocaine exposure (PCE) severely affects brain development, psychology, and behavior in exposed offspring, while altering their susceptibility to drug addiction. however, the mechanisms underlying PCE-induced changes in cocaine-conditioned place preference (CPP) remain unclear. This study demonstrates that PCE attenuates cocaine-induced CPP, a process involving spatial memory and drug reward. We also investigated the dorsal hippocampus (dH), which is closely associated with spatial memory, and the ventral hippocampus (vH), which is linked to motivational reward mechanisms. Results indicate that PCE impairs long-term synaptic plasticity in the dH, suggesting that spatial memory deficits contribute to the attenuation of CPP. In contrast, PCE did not significantly inhibit synaptic plasticity in the vH, indicating that while the vH contributes to addiction susceptibility, it is less affected by prenatal exposure. Notably, acute cocaine exposure increased presynaptic plasticity in the vH regardless of prenatal history. These findings suggest that synaptic impairment in the dH drives spatial memory deficits in PCE offspring, while the vH retains sensitivity to acute drug challenge. This study elucidates the cellular mechanisms underlying PCE-induced cognitive changes and guides future molecular investigations.

title: Vagus Nerve Stimulation as a Potential Therapeutic Strategy for Alcohol Use Disorder.
abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) contributes to approximately 3 million deaths worldwide each year and leads to substantial emotional, financial, and social implications for individuals and their families. AUD leads to multi-system damage, including the immune system, gut microbiome, neuroendocrine pathways, and the brain. Current treatments for AUD, focused primarily on behavioral and pharmaceutical interventions, insufficiently address alcohol's extensive impact on multiple body systems. Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) has shown therapeutic benefits across a spectrum of neurological conditions, including epilepsy, depression, and addictive disorders. More recently, VNS is being investigated as a potential promising adjunctive treatment for AUD, which may complement currently used treatments by targeting many of the body systems dysregulated in AUD. Preclinical and clinical models have evaluated different VNS paradigms, including invasive, noninvasive, and minimally invasive approaches targeting motor and cognitive rehabilitation, withdrawal symptoms, and relapse during abstinence. However, while VNS has many promising potential benefits for improving AUD outcomes, direct evidence that VNS reduces alcohol consumption, alcohol seeking, or craving in AUD remains limited, and there are several logistical and ethical considerations that researchers, clinicians, and policymakers should evaluate before VNS is considered standard of care. Additionally, optimization of VNS parameters, modality (implanted versus noninvasive or minimally invasive), and development of responder biomarkers could better inform patient selection for VNS. Although significant work remains before transitioning VNS into clinical practice, VNS offers an exciting opportunity for adjunctive treatment in AUD that could potentially target multi-system AUD dysfunction.

title: Osteopontin-c expression levels modulate leukemic cell morphological plasticity and transmigration across a blood-brain barrier-on-a-chip model.
authors: Bastos Ana Clara Santos da Fonseca
abstract: Central nervous system infiltration remains a major clinical challenge in B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia, particularly in high-risk subgroups such as KMT2A-rearranged cases. Osteopontin, especially its splice variant Osteopontin-c (OPNc), has been associated with aggressive disease features, including central nervous system involvement, although its functional role in leukemic dissemination remains unclear. Here, we developed a multicellular human blood-brain barrier-on-a-chip model to investigate the contribution of OPNc to leukemic cell transmigration. The microfluidic system recapitulates key structural and functional features of the blood-brain barrier (BBB), including endothelial, pericyte, and astrocyte interactions, and exhibits selective barrier properties. Using this system, we demonstrated that RS4;11 leukemic cells adhere to, infiltrate, and transmigrate across the BBB. Silencing of OPNc significantly reduced leukemic cell migration and invasion in transwell assays and was associated with altered cellular morphology, suggesting impaired migratory plasticity. OPNc-silenced cells showed consistent trends toward reduced infiltration and increased circularity rates. Altogether, these findings evidence a role for OPNc as one of the mediators of leukemic cell behavior associated with CNS infiltration and establishing the BBB-on-a-chip as a physiologically relevant platform for studying leukemic dissemination. Teaser abstract: Central nervous system (CNS) infiltration remains a major challenge in high-risk B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Using a multicellular human blood-brain barrier-on-a-chip, we demonstrate that RS4;11 leukemic cells adhere to and transmigrate across the barrier. OPNc silencing reduced migration and invasion and altered cellular morphology, suggesting impaired migratory plasticity. These findings support OPNc as one of the mediators of leukemic behavior associated with CNS infiltration and establish the BBB-on-a-chip as a physiologically relevant platform to investigate leukemic dissemination.

title: Hippocampal CA2 modulates trace fear conditioning through circuit-specific tuning of CA1 activity.
abstract: Forming associations between temporally separated events depends on pathways linking the CA1, the subiculum (SUB), and the entorhinal cortex. The degree to which this process requires the CA2, which shares extensive connectivity with these regions, remains unknown. Using trace fear conditioning (TFC), in which mice learn to associate a tone and shock separated by a temporal gap, we found that chronic blockade of dorsal CA2 (dCA2) output reduced cue-associated freezing without comparable effects following delay fear conditioning or during contextual fear recall. In contrast, acute inhibition of dCA2→dCA1 projections during either conditioning or recall increased cue-test freezing, whereas inhibition of dCA2→dSUB projections produced no detectable behavioral effect. These manipulations were associated with distinct patterns of hippocampal cFos expression. Fiber photometry showed that dCA2→dCA1 calcium activity exhibited tone-onset modulation during conditioning and late-trace modulation near the time at which shock had occurred during conditioning. Moreover, acute CA2 inhibition during conditioning was associated with persistent tone-onset CA1 modulation during subsequent drug-free recall. Together, these findings identify dCA2 as a contributor to TFC and link dCA2→dCA1 signaling to fear expression and the temporal organization of CA1 activity across learning and recall.

title: Pilocarpine disrupts spontaneous rhythmic inhibitory bursting in the basolateral amygdala, promoting a transition to hyperexcitability.
abstract: The view that seizures arise from an imbalance between excitatory and inhibitory activity, favoring excessive excitation, provides a valid but simplified description of the synaptic interactions underlying seizure initiation. Synchronous, rhythmic activity of inhibitory interneurons is known for imposing order in the activity of neuronal networks, often shaping or giving rise to local and long-range oscillations; disruption of rhythmic inhibitory activity could contribute to network hyperexcitability. In the rat basolateral amygdala (BLA)-a seizure-prone region that is also key to seizure initiation by muscarinic receptor hyperstimulation after organophosphate (OP) exposure-principal neurons display rhythmic, large-amplitude spontaneous IPSC (sIPSC) "bursts" at an average frequency of 0.5 Hz. Here, we used pilocarpine, a muscarinic agonist, to investigate whether disruption of rhythmic inhibitory activity contributes to the mechanisms by which muscarinic receptor hyperstimulation promotes BLA hyperexcitability. In voltage-clamp, pilocarpine suppressed the sIPSC bursts while increasing the background sIPSC activity and the sEPSC-to-sIPSC ratio, in principal neurons; in interneurons, pilocarpine suppressed the rhythmic sEPSC bursts while increasing background sEPSC activity. In current-clamp, pilocarpine produced depolarization and firing bursts in principal cells and sustained, high-frequency firing in interneurons when applied to normal medium or in the presence of CNQX, D-AP5, and bicuculline. Suppression of the sIPSC bursts by pilocarpine, in principal neurons, was mediated via M1 muscarinic receptors. Paraoxon, an OP, also disrupted the sIPSC bursts while increasing background sIPSCs. Thus, muscarinic receptor hyperstimulation in the BLA induces hyperexcitability by disrupting rhythmic inhibition while increasing firing of both principal neurons and interneurons.

title: The UCHL1-HIF-1α Axis Mediates Microglial Metabolic Reprogramming and Neuroinflammation in Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: Microglial-mediated neuroinflammation is a key driver of Parkinson's disease (PD) progression. Ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCHL1) is a neuron-enriched deubiquitinating enzyme, yet its role in microglial immunometabolism and PD pathogenesis remains poorly understood. We investigated the role of UCHL1 using lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated BV2 microglial cells, and brain tissues from a 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-induced mouse model. UCHL1 expression, inflammatory responses, HIF-1α signaling, and glycolytic activity were assessed using Western blotting, RT-qPCR, immunofluorescence, and metabolic assays. The effects of UCHL1 modulation on neuronal survival were examined using conditioned medium transfer experiments. The neuroprotective effects of UCHL1 inhibition in an MPTP-induced mouse model were evaluated by behavioral assessments and immunofluorescence analysis. In BV2 microglia, LPS stimulation partially reduced endogenous UCHL1 expression, the remaining UCHL1 continued to microglial neuroinflammation. Pharmacological inhibition of UCHL1 attenuated inflammatory responses, whereas UCHL1 overexpression exacerbated microglial activation and bystander neuronal injury. UCHL1 promoted glycolytic reprogramming through upregulation of HK2, PKM2, and LDHA. Mechanistically, Inhibition of HIF-1α diminished the increases in pro-inflammatory mediators and glycolytic enzyme expression associated with UCHL1 overexpression. In vivo, immunofluorescence demonstrated UCHL1 expression in activated microglia within the substantia nigra, and UCHL1 inhibition attenuated microglial activation, preserved TH-positive dopaminergic (DA) neurons, and improved motor deficits in MPTP-treated mice. Collectively, our findings identify UCHL1 as a key regulator of microglial immunometabolism in PD. By promoting HIF-1α-dependent glycolytic reprogramming, UCHL1 amplifies neuroinflammation and contributes to DA neurodegeneration, highlighting the UCHL1/HIF-1α/glycolysis axis as a potential therapeutic target for PD.

title: Focus on fear: Questioning the role of threat in fear conditioning.
abstract: There is little doubt that pairing a conditional stimulus with an aversive unconditional stimulus will produce robust changes in behavior caused by later presentations of that conditional stimulus. Recent changes in terminology, however, have obfuscated the psychological processes that might underlie this type of behavioral change. Here, we argue that nomenclature surrounding this type of aversive learning should be standardized to reflect the detailed and historical work that has defined 'fear' as a robust and replicable conditional response following aversive conditioning.

title: Hantavirus infection and the boundaries of autoimmunity: Vascular immunopathology, autoimmune-like mimicry, and post-infectious phenomena.
abstract: Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne RNA viruses causing acute systemic vascular syndromes, principally haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Although primarily infectious, hantavirus disease may generate vascular, renal, haematological, and systemic phenotypes that overlap with immune-mediated disorders. This Review critically examines the boundary between infection-driven immunopathology and autoimmunity. Hantavirus infection involves endothelial dysfunction, innate antiviral sensing, interferon responses, cytokine and chemokine amplification, complement activation, immunothrombosis, and adaptive immune responses, whose expression is further influenced by virus-, host-, and tissue-specific factors. These mechanisms contribute to the marked heterogeneity of clinical disease and may reproduce autoimmune-like clinical and laboratory features, but do not, in themselves, establish sustained loss of immune tolerance. Current evidence is substantially stronger for acute infection-associated immunopathology and phenotypic mimicry than for persistent autoreactivity or causally attributable post-infectious autoimmune disease. Reported autoimmune phenomena remain uncommon and predominantly case-based, while longitudinal, antigen-specific, and epidemiological evidence is limited. Persistent or recurrent manifestations after resolution of infection therefore require additional serological, histopathological, or other objective evidence of sustained immune dysregulation. Hantavirus infection thus provides a clinically informative model for distinguishing antiviral immunopathology from autoimmune-like mimicry and rare possible post-infectious autoimmunity, with direct implications for diagnosis and therapeutic restraint.
